title: When you're sick
goal: Describe what's wrong at a pharmacy or clinic, understand the advice you're given, and use the prohibition form -지 마세요, which hasn't appeared until now.
bekal: naming body parts and saying which part hurts
describing common symptoms at the pharmacy
telling someone not to do something with -지 마세요
expressing sympathy with the right phrases

dialogs.title: 대화 — At the pharmacy
dialogs.intro: Ani has been feeling unwell since yesterday. Notice that the pharmacist's advice is all polite commands, and the prohibitions use a new form.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: My throat has hurt since yesterday. And I have a slight fever too.
lines.literal: yesterday-from — throat — subject — hurts. and — fever — also — a-little — exists.

lines.speaker: 약사:
lines.id: Do you have a cough too?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, the cough is bad at night. I couldn't sleep.
lines.literal: yes, night-at — cough — subject — severe. sleep — object — couldn't — slept.

lines.speaker: 약사:
lines.id: It looks like a cold. Take this medicine three times a day.
lines.literal: cold-subject — caught — thing — seems. this — medicine — object — day-per — three — times — please-eat.

lines.speaker: 약사:
lines.id: After meals. Don't take it on an empty stomach.
lines.literal: meal — after-at — please-eat. empty — stomach-on — eat — don't.

lines.speaker: 약사:
lines.id: Get plenty of rest today. Don't drink cold water.
lines.literal: today — as-for — deeply — please-rest. cold — water — drink — don't.

lines.speaker: 약사:
lines.id: Four thousand won. Get well soon.

notes: **아프다 is used for the body part that hurts, not for the person.** The correct form is 목**이** 아파요 ("the throat hurts"), not 저는 목을 아파요. The body part is the subject, with 이/가 — just as in English "my throat hurts". Same pattern as 배가 고파요 ("the stomach is hungry" = I'm hungry).

**어디가 아파요?, not 어디 아파요?** The particle 가 is required here because the body part is the subject. Compare unit 3: 어디에 있어요? takes 에 because it asks for a location. Two questions that sound alike, two different particles.

**감기 covers far more than English "flu".** It includes a runny nose, cough, sore throat and mild fever — anything you'd call "a cold". 감기에 걸렸어요 = "I caught a cold", using 걸리다, which in unit 13 meant "to take (time)". Same word, different job.
**약을 먹다, not 약을 마시다.** In Korea medicine is "eaten", even liquid medicine. The honorific form is 약을 드세요, and that's what you'll hear from the pharmacist.
**하루에 세 번 = three times a day.** Note the order: the time unit comes first with 에, then the number. 일주일에 두 번 (twice a week), 한 달에 한 번 (once a month). The reverse of the English order.
**전에 and 후에 go after the noun.** 식사 **전에** (before the meal), 식사 **후에** (after the meal). Like the place words in unit 3, Korean time words come after what they refer to.

**푹 쉬세요 is the standard thing to say to someone who's ill.** 푹 means "deeply, fully", and it almost always pairs with 쉬다 and 자다. Together with 빨리 나으세요 ("get well soon"), these are sentences you must have.
**나으세요 comes from 낫다 (to get better), an irregular ㅅ verb.** The ㅅ drops before a vowel: 낫다 → 나아요 → 나으세요. The group is small but contains common words: 짓다 (to build) → 지어요, 붓다 (to swell) → 부어요.

grammars.title: -지 마세요 — don't
body: The polite prohibition. Attach **-지 마세요** straight to the verb stem, whether it ends in a vowel or a consonant.
after: ⚠️ **Don't use 안 to forbid.** 안 가세요 isn't "don't go" but "you aren't going" — a statement, not a prohibition. To forbid, the only correct form is -지 마세요.
**To include yourself and others** ("let's not…") there's -지 맙시다, but it's rare in conversation. People more often say 하지 말까요? ("shall we not?").
**걱정하지 마세요** ("don't worry") is worth learning whole — it's one of the most-used comforting phrases.

grammars.title: Body parts and symptoms
body: The pattern is always **body part + 이/가 + 아파요**.
after: **Common symptoms:** 열이 있어요 (I have a fever), 기침을 해요 (I'm coughing), 콧물이 나요 (my nose is running), 어지러워요 (I'm dizzy), 토할 것 같아요 (I feel sick), 설사를 해요 (I have diarrhea), 몸살이 났어요 (I ache all over from exhaustion).
**몸살 has no English equivalent.** It means aching all over from exhaustion or stress, is considered an illness in its own right in Korea, and is a perfectly valid reason to miss work.

blocks.title: Pharmacies and clinics in Korea
items: A **약국** (pharmacy) has a green sign with 약 on it. For minor complaints — colds, headaches, small cuts — the pharmacist can give medicine without a prescription, and it's the fastest route.
**병원** is used for both clinics and hospitals; small clinics are usually called 의원 or named after their specialty: 내과 (internal medicine), 이비인후과 (ENT), 치과 (dentist), 피부과 (dermatology).

⚠️ As a foreign student or worker on a long-term visa, you must join the national health insurance (**건강보험**) — and with it, treatment becomes very cheap. Bring your foreign resident card (외국인등록증) every time you see a doctor.
